y-m-71-01.title: Is there only one point at distance 10 from the focus?
y-m-71-01.topic: Focus and directrix of a parabola
y-m-71-01.goal: In a solution that finds points using the condition on the distance from a point on a parabola to the focus, find the line that missed the symmetry, and work out for yourself how many points satisfy the condition in all.
y-m-71-01.material: Consider the parabola y² = 8x (read: y squared equals eight x) on the coordinate plane. Let F be the focus of this parabola, and let the point P(x, y) be a point on the parabola. A student solved the problem of finding all points P with distance PF equal to 10 as shown below. The units of the coordinates are all the same, and lengths are written without units.
y-m-71-01.thinking.0: Checking the validity of a solution line by line
y-m-71-01.thinking.1: Working out how many points satisfy the condition
y-m-71-01.thinking.2: Judging whether a solution exists from the range of possible values
y-m-71-01.prereq.0: Assumption: this task is set at an advanced high-school level, to be solved after already learning the elective course 'Geometry' (conic sections, plane vectors, solids and space coordinates); 'H3' is only a difficulty label for this production batch and does not mean the course is assigned to a particular grade. Definition of a parabola (focus and directrix), focus and directrix of the form y²=4px, distance formula between two points
y-m-71-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in the solution that is wrong.
y-m-71-01.s.s1.hint.0: Put the expression of each line directly into the next line, and compare whether the number of cases was reduced when going from an earlier line to a later one.
y-m-71-01.s.s1.hint.1: Write all the values y can take when x = 8 is put into the equation of the parabola.
y-m-71-01.s.s1.line.0: From the form y² = 4px, 4p = 8, so p = 2, the focus F is (2, 0), and the directrix is x = −2.
y-m-71-01.s.s1.line.1: For a point P(x, y) on the parabola, PF equals the distance from P to the directrix, so PF = x + 2.
y-m-71-01.s.s1.line.2: PF = 10, so x + 2 = 10, that is, x = 8.
y-m-71-01.s.s1.line.3: y² = 8 · 8 = 64, so y = 8, and the only point that satisfies the condition is P(8, 8).
y-m-71-01.s.s1.line.4: Therefore the point P with PF = 10 is (8, 8).
y-m-71-01.s.s1.explain: Lines 1 to 3 are correct. In line 4, if y² = 64 then y = 8 or y = −8. A parabola is symmetric about the x-axis, so both points (8, 8) and (8, −8) satisfy the condition. Line 5 simply inherited the omission of line 4.
y-m-71-01.s.s2.prompt: Enter 2 different points P(x, y) on the parabola with integer coordinates that satisfy PF = 10. (The focus F is (2, 0).)
y-m-71-01.s.s2.hint.0: First write the relationship between x and y as an equation using the condition that the point is on the parabola.
y-m-71-01.s.s2.hint.1: Choose one x, check whether y comes out as an integer, and calculate directly the distance from that point to F.
y-m-71-01.s.s2.ok.c1: The point is on the parabola y² = 8x.
y-m-71-01.s.s2.fail.c1: The point is not on the parabola y² = 8x.
y-m-71-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The distance to F(2, 0) is not 10.
y-m-71-01.s.s2.explain: The only points that satisfy both conditions are (8, 8) and (8, −8). x is fixed as one value and only the sign of y has two possibilities.
y-m-71-01.s.s3.prompt: How many points P on the same parabola have PF = 1?
y-m-71-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write PF as an expression in x and check the range of values x can take for points on the parabola.
y-m-71-01.s.s3.hint.1: Calculate directly the distance from the vertex O(0, 0) to F.
y-m-71-01.s.s3.o.a: One. The vertex O is such a point
y-m-71-01.s.s3.r.a: If you calculate PF at the vertex directly, it is not 1. You guessed the nearest point without calculating.
y-m-71-01.s.s3.o.b: Two. Two points symmetric about the x-axis
y-m-71-01.s.s3.r.b: You carried over the conclusion 'two symmetric points' from the previous step as it was. You must first check whether the value of x is possible.
y-m-71-01.s.s3.o.c: Cannot be known. It cannot be decided from the shape alone
y-m-71-01.s.s3.r.c: The expression PF = x + 2 lets you decide the range of possible values. This is not a case of lacking information.
y-m-71-01.s.s3.o.d: None. PF is always at least 2
y-m-71-01.s.s3.r.d: x + 2 becomes 2 at the smallest value x can take. This is a judgment that examined the possible range of the distance.
y-m-71-01.s.s3.explain: PF = x + 2, and on the parabola x ≥ 0, so PF ≥ 2. For PF = 1 we would need x = −1, but then y² = −8 and there is no real y. A distance condition can have no solution at all.

y-m-71-02.title: Are points with a constant sum of distances always an ellipse?
y-m-71-02.topic: Definition of an ellipse (the sum of distances to two points)
y-m-71-02.goal: Find the condition needed for the set of points with a constant sum of distances to two points to be an ellipse, and say what figure results when the condition is lacking or at the boundary.
y-m-71-02.material: On the coordinate plane there are two points F(−4, 0) and F'(4, 0) (read: F and F prime). The distance between the two points is 8. A point P(x, y) moves so that PF + PF' = s. Here s is a positive constant, and lengths are written without units.
y-m-71-02.thinking.0: Finding the condition hidden in the definition
y-m-71-02.thinking.1: Judging whether the information is sufficient
y-m-71-02.thinking.2: Reasoning about the figure in the boundary case
y-m-71-02.prereq.0: Assumption: this task is set at an advanced high-school level, to be solved after already learning the elective course 'Geometry' (conic sections, plane vectors, solids and space coordinates); 'H3' is only a difficulty label for this production batch and does not mean the course is assigned to a particular grade. Definition and standard form of an ellipse, distance between two points, relationships among the three side lengths of a triangle
y-m-71-02.s.s1.prompt: Without knowing the value of s, can we say that the figure drawn by the point P is an ellipse?
y-m-71-02.s.s1.hint.0: Put a few values into s and work out whether such a point P exists at all.
y-m-71-02.s.s1.hint.1: Write what relationship holds among the three side lengths when the points P, F and F' are joined to form a triangle.
y-m-71-02.s.s1.o.a: We cannot say. If s is 8 or less, it is not an ellipse
y-m-71-02.s.s1.r.a: You pointed out that, in addition to the definition, s must be compared with the distance between the two points.
y-m-71-02.s.s1.o.b: We can say. As long as the sum is constant, it is always an ellipse
y-m-71-02.s.s1.r.b: You remembered the definition only up to 'the sum is constant'. Have you ever compared the size of the sum with the distance between the two points?
y-m-71-02.s.s1.o.c: We cannot say. It is decided by the positions of the two points alone
y-m-71-02.s.s1.r.c: s is a fixed constant and affects the shape. Test what changes when you change s.
y-m-71-02.s.s1.o.d: We can say. Whatever positive number s is, P exists
y-m-71-02.s.s1.r.d: You treated 'P exists' and 'it is an ellipse' as the same thing. Even if it exists, the shape may not be an ellipse.
y-m-71-02.s.s1.explain: PF + PF' ≥ FF' = 8, so if s < 8 there is no such point P, and if s = 8 the points are on segment FF'. It is an ellipse only when s > 8. So more information about s is needed.
y-m-71-02.s.s2.prompt: When s = 10, enter 2 different points P(x, y) with integer coordinates that satisfy PF + PF' = 10.
y-m-71-02.s.s2.hint.0: Start by choosing points on the axes and calculate PF and PF' for each.
y-m-71-02.s.s2.hint.1: If the sum of the two distances for the point you chose is greater than 10, move the point closer to the two foci; if smaller, move it farther away.
y-m-71-02.s.s2.ok.c1: The sum of the distances to the two points is 10.
y-m-71-02.s.s2.fail.c1: The sum of the distances to the two points is not 10.
y-m-71-02.s.s2.explain: The only points with integer coordinates are the four points (5, 0), (−5, 0), (0, 3) and (0, −3). Starting on the axes lets you add the distances right away. There are far more points on the ellipse that are not integers.
y-m-71-02.s.s3.prompt: When s = 8, what figure do all the points P satisfying PF + PF' = 8 form?
y-m-71-02.s.s3.hint.0: Calculate PF + PF' at a point on segment FF' (for example the origin).
y-m-71-02.s.s3.hint.1: Calculate the sum at a point off the segment (for example (0, 1)) and compare it with 8.
y-m-71-02.s.s3.o.a: An ellipse with foci F and F'
y-m-71-02.s.s3.r.a: If the sum is 8, it equals the distance between the two points. Work out whether the sum must be greater than that for an ellipse.
y-m-71-02.s.s3.o.b: Only the two points F and F'
y-m-71-02.s.s3.r.b: Calculate the sum at another point on the segment. What is the sum at the middle point O(0, 0)?
y-m-71-02.s.s3.r.c: If P is on the segment, PF + PF' is exactly 8. You separated out the boundary case.
y-m-71-02.s.s3.o.d: No points at all (the empty set)
y-m-71-02.s.s3.r.d: Calculate the sum directly at one point on the segment. You did not test whether there really are no points.
y-m-71-02.s.s3.explain: If P is on segment FF', then PF + PF' = 8, and if it is off the segment, the sum is greater than 8 because of the relationship among the side lengths of a triangle. So the figure when s = 8 is a segment.

y-m-71-03.title: If it meets at only one point, is it a tangent?
y-m-71-03.topic: Intersections of a hyperbola and a line, tangent lines
y-m-71-03.goal: Find for yourself the case where the generalization 'a line that meets at only one point is a tangent' breaks for a hyperbola, and explain why, connecting it to the asymptotes.
y-m-71-03.material: Consider the hyperbola H: x²/9 − y²/16 = 1 (read: x squared over 9 minus y squared over 16 equals 1). The asymptotes of H are y = (4/3)x and y = −(4/3)x. Lines are written in the form px + qy = r (p, q and r are integers and p and q are not both 0). A student said, 'For an ellipse, a line that meets it at only one point is a tangent. So for H too, a line that meets it at only one point must be a tangent.'
y-m-71-03.thinking.0: Identifying the conditions for a counterexample to a generalization
y-m-71-03.thinking.1: Making several examples that satisfy the conditions
y-m-71-03.thinking.2: Explaining the difference between a tangent and a line that meets at one point
y-m-71-03.prereq.0: Assumption: this task is set at an advanced high-school level, to be solved after already learning the elective course 'Geometry' (conic sections, plane vectors, solids and space coordinates); 'H3' is only a difficulty label for this production batch and does not mean the course is assigned to a particular grade. Standard form and asymptotes of a hyperbola, the meaning of the discriminant when a line and a conic are combined
y-m-71-03.s.s1.prompt: What kind of line should you look for to test whether this student's statement is always right for H too?
y-m-71-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write the claim split into 'if condition A then conclusion B'. What are A and B?
y-m-71-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether the claim breaks if there is even just one example.
y-m-71-03.s.s1.o.a: Some line that meets H at two different points
y-m-71-03.s.s1.r.a: The claim is about lines that meet 'at only one point'. A line that meets at two points is not an object of the claim.
y-m-71-03.s.s1.o.b: A non-tangent line that meets H at only one point
y-m-71-03.s.s1.r.b: You tried to find a line that satisfies the first condition 'meets at one point' but breaks the second condition 'is a tangent'.
y-m-71-03.s.s1.o.c: Any one of the tangents of H
y-m-71-03.s.s1.r.c: A tangent meeting at one point is an example that agrees with the claim. Collecting more such examples cannot tell you the claim is wrong.
y-m-71-03.s.s1.o.d: Some line that never meets H
y-m-71-03.s.s1.r.d: A line that does not meet H does not satisfy the claim's condition (meeting at one point) in the first place.
y-m-71-03.s.s1.explain: To show that 'if A then B' is wrong, you need an example that satisfies A but does not satisfy B. Here A is 'meets at only one point' and B is 'is a tangent'.
y-m-71-03.s.s2.prompt: Among the lines px + qy = r, enter 2 different lines that meet H at exactly one point but are not tangents. (|p|, |q| ≤ 20, |r| ≤ 100. The same line written with proportional integers counts as one line.)
y-m-71-03.s.s2.hint.0: Rewrite the line in the form y = mx + k and substitute it into the equation of H; calculate whether there is an m that makes the coefficient of x² in the expression in x equal to 0.
y-m-71-03.s.s2.hint.1: Compare such an m with the slope of the asymptotes of H, and write the slope as a ratio of p and q so that p and q are integers.
y-m-71-03.s.s2.fail.c1: If p and q are both 0, it is not a line.
y-m-71-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Keep p and q at most 20 and r at most 100 in absolute value.
y-m-71-03.s.s2.ok.c3: It is a line that meets at only one point (slope condition).
y-m-71-03.s.s2.fail.c3: This line is not of the kind that meets at only one point (or it is a tangent).
y-m-71-03.s.s2.ok.c4: It does not pass through the origin, so it really meets H.
y-m-71-03.s.s2.fail.c4: If r = 0, it is the asymptote itself and does not meet H.
y-m-71-03.s.s2.explain: Example: 4x + 3y = 6 meets H at only one point but is not a tangent. This is because the slope of this line is the same as the slope of the asymptote y = −(4/3)x. 5x + 3y = 9 or x = 3 meet at one point and are tangents, so they are not counterexamples.
y-m-71-03.s.s3.prompt: Explain in 2 to 3 sentences why the line you chose is not a tangent even though it meets H at only one point, using the equation of your line or the asymptote and slope.
y-m-71-03.s.s3.hint.0: First write in one sentence which value in the equation of that line is the same as the asymptote's.
y-m-71-03.s.s3.hint.1: Add one line on how the degree of the expression in x changes.
y-m-71-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does my explanation include the equation or slope of the line I chose?
y-m-71-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I distinguish in my own words that 'meets at one point' and 'is tangent' are not the same?
y-m-71-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I think about how the system of equations would have been different if it were a tangent?
y-m-71-03.s.s3.model.0: The line 4x + 3y = 6 has the same slope as the asymptote y = −(4/3)x, so they are parallel. When substituted, the coefficient of x² disappears and it becomes a linear equation with only one solution, so it meets at only one point, but it is not a quadratic equation with a double root, so it is not a tangent.
y-m-71-03.s.s3.model.1: A line parallel to an asymptote meets H at one point, but it differs from a tangent, whose discriminant is 0. A tangent meets H at the point of tangency and stays on one side of the curve, whereas this line crosses through one branch of H.

y-m-71-04.title: If we divide both sides by a, is b = c?
y-m-71-04.goal: Show by a counterexample that equal dot products do not make two vectors equal, and work out how many remain when a condition on size is added.
y-m-71-04.material: The plane vectors are a = (2, 1) and c = (1, 3). Jisu said, 'Since a · b = a · c, dividing both sides by a gives b = c.' (The dot means the dot product.) b has the form b = (b1, b2) and its components are real numbers.
y-m-71-04.thinking.0: Testing whether rules of calculation with numbers can be carried straight over to the dot product of vectors
y-m-71-04.thinking.1: Making several vectors that satisfy a condition
y-m-71-04.thinking.2: Reasoning about the number of solutions when a condition is added
y-m-71-04.prereq.0: Assumption: this task is set at an advanced high-school level, to be solved after already learning the elective course 'Geometry' (conic sections, plane vectors, solids and space coordinates); 'H3' is only a difficulty label for this production batch and does not mean the course is assigned to a particular grade. Component form of plane vectors, computing the dot product with components, the magnitude of a vector
y-m-71-04.s.s1.prompt: What is the surest way to check whether Jisu's conclusion 'b = c' always holds?
y-m-71-04.s.s1.hint.0: Solve a · b = a · c in components and write it as an equation between b1 and b2.
y-m-71-04.s.s1.hint.1: Choose one b that satisfies that equation and compare it with c.
y-m-71-04.s.s1.o.a: Put in many b and see whether they are all b = c
y-m-71-04.s.s1.r.a: Collecting examples and looking only at the ones that fit cannot show 'always'. In particular, the examples you pick may be biased to one side.
y-m-71-04.s.s1.o.b: Check that since a is not the zero vector, we can divide both sides
y-m-71-04.s.s1.r.b: You carried the cancelling rule used in multiplication of numbers straight over to the dot product. The dot product is an operation that turns vectors into a number.
y-m-71-04.s.s1.o.c: Look for b with a · b = a · c and b ≠ c
y-m-71-04.s.s1.r.c: You used the fact that to break 'always', one example that satisfies the condition but has a wrong conclusion is enough.
y-m-71-04.s.s1.o.d: First compare whether b and c have the same size
y-m-71-04.s.s1.r.d: Having the same size is a necessary condition for b = c, but you should first check whether it follows from the given condition.
y-m-71-04.s.s1.explain: To break 'it always holds', one example that satisfies the condition a · b = a · c while b ≠ c is enough.
y-m-71-04.s.s2.prompt: Enter 3 different b = (b1, b2) with integer components that satisfy a · b = a · c but b ≠ c. (|b1| ≤ 5)
y-m-71-04.s.s2.hint.0: First calculate the value of a · c by putting in c, then write a · b in components and set them equal.
y-m-71-04.s.s2.hint.1: Choose b1 and check how b2 is determined, then check that b is different from c.
y-m-71-04.s.s2.ok.c1: a · b is equal to a · c.
y-m-71-04.s.s2.fail.c1: a · b is not equal to a · c (= 5).
y-m-71-04.s.s2.fail.c2: b is the same as c. Find a different vector.
y-m-71-04.s.s2.explain: a · c = 2·1 + 1·3 = 5, so it is enough that 2b1 + b2 = 5. There are as many as you like, such as (0, 5), (2, 1), (3, −1). All such b have the same component in the direction of a as c and differ only in the component perpendicular to a.
y-m-71-04.s.s3.prompt: If you add |b| = |c| (the size of b equals the size of c) as well, how many b are there in all with a · b = a · c and b ≠ c? (The components are real numbers.)
y-m-71-04.s.s3.hint.0: Substitute b2 = 5 − 2b1 into b1² + b2² = 10 to make an expression in b1.
y-m-71-04.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether c itself is among the solutions found and exclude it.
y-m-71-04.s.s3.r.a: You thought b = c is the only one. Solve the two equations together and calculate how many values of b1 come out.
y-m-71-04.s.s3.r.b: You recognized that the two conditions almost determine b. If you solve it directly, one more remains besides b = c.
y-m-71-04.s.s3.r.c: You matched it to the 2 solutions of the two equations. Did you check whether one of them is c itself?
y-m-71-04.s.s3.r.d: You carried over the conclusion for when there is one condition. Since there is one more equation, work out how the solutions change.
y-m-71-04.s.s3.explain: Combining 2b1 + b2 = 5 and b1² + b2² = 10 gives (1, 3) and (3, −1). (1, 3) is c itself, so the only b different from c is (3, −1). This b is the vector c reflected across the line in the direction of a.

y-m-71-05.title: If the range of the coefficients changes, what figure does the point draw?
y-m-71-05.topic: Linear combinations of plane vectors and figures
y-m-71-05.goal: Predict that the figure drawn by the point P changes with the conditions on the coefficients x and y in OP = x·OA + y·OB, confirm that the region becomes flat when the two vectors are parallel, and then build points that fit an area condition yourself.
y-m-71-05.material: Let O be the origin of the coordinate plane, and write the position of a point P as the vector OP = x·OA + y·OB (read: vector OP equals x times vector OA plus y times vector OB). x and y are real numbers and the conditions change at each step. Lengths are written without units.
y-m-71-05.thinking.0: Re-predicting the figure when the conditions change
y-m-71-05.thinking.1: Reasoning about how whether two vectors are parallel affects the region
y-m-71-05.prereq.0: Assumption: this task is set at an advanced high-school level, to be solved after already learning the elective course 'Geometry' (conic sections, plane vectors, solids and space coordinates); 'H3' is only a difficulty label for this production batch and does not mean the course is assigned to a particular grade. Component form of plane vectors, scalar multiples and addition, the line through two points, the area of a parallelogram
y-m-71-05.s.s1.prompt: The conditions and points are revealed step by step. At each step, predict the figure (or region) that P draws.
y-m-71-05.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, choose two or three pairs (x, y) that satisfy the conditions and calculate the coordinates of P directly.
y-m-71-05.s.s1.hint.1: In step 3, compare the components to see what relationship there is between OA and OB.
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.0.info: A(2, 0), B(0, 2), and x and y are all real numbers satisfying x + y = 1.
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.0.after: P = (2x, 2y) and x + y = 1, so the points are on the line x + y = 2. x and y may be negative, so it is the whole line AB.
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You thought about it including the fact that x and y can be negative.
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You thought only of the case where x and y are 0 or more. The condition has no restriction on signs.
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: x + y = 1 is a single equation, so it cannot fill a wide part of the plane. Work out how many degrees of freedom the equation leaves.
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.1.info: Add one more condition for the same A and B. x + y = 1 and x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now what figure does P draw?
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.1.after: A point such as x = 2, y = −1 is left out because it violates y ≥ 0. The points left are those with x and y at least 0 and sum 1, that is, segment AB. It is right to narrow the prediction of the previous step to fit the condition.
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The whole line AB as it was
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You did not check which points the new condition removes. What is y when x = 2?
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You judged that only the cases where the coefficients are not negative remain, leaving only the part between A and B.
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Only the two points A and B
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Test whether the points where x is between 0 and 1 also satisfy the condition.
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.2.info: Change the vectors to A(2, 1) and B(4, 2), and the condition is 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1. (There is no x + y = 1 condition.)
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the area of the region P moves in?
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.2.after: OB = 2·OA, so P = (x + 2y)·OA. x + 2y varies from 0 to 3, so the region is the segment from the origin to (6, 3), and its area is 0. When the vectors are parallel, the parallelogram becomes flat.
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You noticed that B = 2A, so the two vectors have the same direction.
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 10 (the product of the length √5 of OA and the length 2√5 of OB)
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You assumed a rectangle with the two vectors perpendicular. You did not check the angle between the two vectors.
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.2.o.c: 4 (the product of the first components 2 and the second components 2 of the two vectors)
y-m-71-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You multiplied only some of the components. The area of a parallelogram is determined by a quantity made by the directions of the two sides.
y-m-71-05.s.s1.reflect: Going from step 1 to step 2 and from step 2 to step 3, what changed the figure? Say separately what was a change in the condition on the coefficients and what was a change in the vectors themselves.
y-m-71-05.s.s2.prompt: OA = (3, 0), and B(b1, b2) has integer coordinates. Enter 3 different points B for which the parallelogram drawn by P = x·OA + y·OB for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1 has area exactly 6. (|b1| ≤ 5)
y-m-71-05.s.s2.hint.0: Write the area of the parallelogram formed by OA and OB by taking OA as the base and finding the height.
y-m-71-05.s.s2.hint.1: Move B to two or three positions and check whether the area changes when you change b1.
y-m-71-05.s.s2.ok.c1: The area of the parallelogram is 6.
y-m-71-05.s.s2.fail.c1: The area of the parallelogram is not 6.
y-m-71-05.s.s2.explain: The base OA has length 3 and the height is |b2|, so the area is 3|b2|. If 3|b2| = 6, then b2 = 2 or −2 and b1 is free. So there are many answers.
y-m-71-05.s.s3.prompt: In s2, why does the area stay the same whatever integer you change b1 to?
y-m-71-05.s.s3.hint.0: In the parallelogram, take OA as the base and observe the height as you slide the position of B in the x-axis direction.
y-m-71-05.s.s3.hint.1: Compare how the height changes when you change b2.
y-m-71-05.s.s3.o.a: The larger b1 is, the more the parallelogram slants and the smaller the area becomes
y-m-71-05.s.s3.r.a: You looked only at the slant and did not consider the base and height. The base and height can stay the same even when it slants.
y-m-71-05.s.s3.o.b: The area is determined only by the length of OB, so if b1 gets larger the area gets larger
y-m-71-05.s.s3.r.b: You decided the area by one side length. You missed that the angle between the two sides changes too.
y-m-71-05.s.s3.o.c: The area is determined only by the angle between the two vectors, so it has nothing to do with b1
y-m-71-05.s.s3.r.c: You thought equal angles mean equal areas. The side lengths also go into the area.
y-m-71-05.s.s3.o.d: The base OA is the same and the height is determined by the size of the y-coordinate of B
y-m-71-05.s.s3.r.d: You understood which component determines the area in terms of the base and height of the figure.
y-m-71-05.s.s3.explain: OA is on the x-axis, so the base is 3 and the height is the distance |b2| from B to the x-axis. Changing b1 pushes B parallel to the x-axis, so the height does not change.

y-m-71-06.title: How many points satisfy the equal-distance conditions?
y-m-71-06.topic: Distances from a point to axes and planes in space coordinates
y-m-71-06.goal: Tell apart the distance to an axis and the distance to a coordinate plane in space coordinates, and design points that satisfy both distance conditions at once.
y-m-71-06.material: In space coordinates the x-axis, y-axis and z-axis are perpendicular to one another, and the xy-plane is the plane z = 0. There is a point P(3, 4, 12). 'The distance from a point to a coordinate axis' is the length of the perpendicular from the point to the axis, and 'the distance from a point to a coordinate plane' is the length of the perpendicular to the plane. Lengths are written without units.
y-m-71-06.thinking.0: Telling apart the distance to an axis and the distance to a plane
y-m-71-06.thinking.1: Designing points that satisfy two conditions at once
y-m-71-06.thinking.2: Explaining the relationship between the number of conditions and the degrees of freedom
y-m-71-06.prereq.0: Assumption: this task is set at an advanced high-school level, to be solved after already learning the elective course 'Geometry' (conic sections, plane vectors, solids and space coordinates); 'H3' is only a difficulty label for this production batch and does not mean the course is assigned to a particular grade. Space coordinates (coordinates of a point), distance between two points, the meaning of the coordinate axes and coordinate planes
y-m-71-06.s.s1.prompt: What is the distance from the point P(3, 4, 12) to the z-axis?
y-m-71-06.s.s1.hint.0: Write the coordinates of the point on the z-axis that has the same z-coordinate as P.
y-m-71-06.s.s1.hint.1: Compare in which component the difference between that point and P arises.
y-m-71-06.s.s1.r.a: You used the fact that the nearest point on the z-axis is (0, 0, 12) and found the distance from only the x and y components.
y-m-71-06.s.s1.r.b: You read the z-coordinate directly. The z-coordinate is related to the distance to the xy-plane.
y-m-71-06.s.s1.r.c: You found the distance to the origin. The origin is not the nearest point on the axis.
y-m-71-06.s.s1.r.d: You simply added x and y. A distance is the length of a perpendicular, so you must use the Pythagorean theorem.
y-m-71-06.s.s1.explain: The point on the z-axis nearest to P is (0, 0, 12), and the distance is √(3² + 4²) = 5. The z-coordinate 12 is the distance to the xy-plane.
y-m-71-06.s.s2.prompt: Enter 4 different points Q(x, y, z) with integer coordinates whose distance to the z-axis is 5 and whose distance to the xy-plane is 12.
y-m-71-06.s.s2.hint.0: Write what expression in x and y the distance 5 to the z-axis becomes, and find several integer pairs that satisfy it.
y-m-71-06.s.s2.hint.1: Check how many values of z the distance 12 to the xy-plane allows.
y-m-71-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The distance to the z-axis is 5.
y-m-71-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The distance to the z-axis is not 5.
y-m-71-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The distance to the xy-plane is 12.
y-m-71-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The distance to the xy-plane is not 12.
y-m-71-06.s.s2.explain: There are 12 integer pairs satisfying x² + y² = 25, and z is 12 or −12, so there are 24 points with integer coordinates in all. The two conditions are attached separately to different coordinates.
y-m-71-06.s.s3.prompt: Explain, using the points you made as examples, why so many points satisfy the conditions although there are only two. Also write how the way of choosing x and y differs from the way of choosing z.
y-m-71-06.s.s3.hint.0: Write what set of points x² + y² = 25 is in the xy-plane.
y-m-71-06.s.s3.hint.1: Write how many values of z the condition on z allows.
y-m-71-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I explain separately the condition that decides x and y and the condition that decides z?
y-m-71-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I include at least one coordinate of a point I made as an example?
y-m-71-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I think about how many more points there would be if the coordinates did not have to be integers?
y-m-71-06.s.s3.model.0: If the distance to the z-axis is 5, then x² + y² = 25, so seen in the xy-plane the points lie on a circle of radius 5. There are many such points, like (3, 4) or (4, −3), and if the distance to the xy-plane is 12, then z is 12 or −12, two cases, so the points multiply.
y-m-71-06.s.s3.model.1: We have to fix the three values x, y and z, but there are only two conditions, on the sum of x² and y² and on the absolute value of z, so the point can move freely. Besides 3² + 4² = 25 there are points with 5² + 0² = 25, and z is 12 or −12, so there are as many as 24 different points.

y-m-71-07.title: If a line is perpendicular to two lines, is it perpendicular to the plane too?
y-m-71-07.topic: Perpendicularity of a line and a plane (space coordinates)
y-m-71-07.goal: Find the missing condition in the judgment 'if a line is perpendicular to two lines in a plane, it is perpendicular to that plane', and build with coordinates a counterexample in which the condition is lacking.
y-m-71-07.material: In space coordinates the xy-plane α is the plane z = 0. Line m1 is the x-axis with direction vector (1, 0, 0), and line m2 is the line through the point (0, 1, 0) parallel to the x-axis with direction vector (2, 0, 0). Both lines are in α. Let the direction vector of line l be d = (d1, d2, d3) (not the zero vector), and a student solved it by saying, 'l is perpendicular to both m1 and m2, so it is perpendicular to α.'
y-m-71-07.thinking.0: Finding the hidden condition in an argument
y-m-71-07.thinking.1: Making an example that satisfies the conditions but has a wrong conclusion
y-m-71-07.thinking.2: Choosing the extra information needed for the conclusion
y-m-71-07.prereq.0: Assumption: this task is set at an advanced high-school level, to be solved after already learning the elective course 'Geometry' (conic sections, plane vectors, solids and space coordinates); 'H3' is only a difficulty label for this production batch and does not mean the course is assigned to a particular grade. Component form and dot product of vectors in space coordinates, perpendicularity and parallelism of two lines, the meaning of a line being perpendicular to a plane
y-m-71-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line in the student's solution where the justification falls short.
y-m-71-07.s.s1.hint.0: Write the equations from line 2 and line 3 side by side and compare whether they are different pieces of information.
y-m-71-07.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether d = (0, 1, 0) satisfies line 2 and line 3 and whether that line is perpendicular to α.
y-m-71-07.s.s1.line.0: Let the direction vector of line l be d = (d1, d2, d3).
y-m-71-07.s.s1.line.1: It is perpendicular to the direction vector (1, 0, 0) of m1, so d1 = 0.
y-m-71-07.s.s1.line.2: It is also perpendicular to the direction vector (2, 0, 0) of m2, so 2 · d1 = 0.
y-m-71-07.s.s1.line.3: If a line is perpendicular to two lines in a plane, it is perpendicular to that plane, so l ⟂ α.
y-m-71-07.s.s1.line.4: Therefore d must have the form (0, 0, d3).
y-m-71-07.s.s1.explain: Lines 2 and 3 are correct, but line 3 is the same equation as line 2 (d1 = 0). Line 4 states, without its condition, something that holds only when the two lines in the plane are not parallel to each other. So line 5 is not guaranteed either.
y-m-71-07.s.s2.prompt: Enter 3 direction vectors with integer components, in different directions, of lines l for which d is perpendicular to the direction vectors of both m1 and m2 but l is not perpendicular to α. (|d2|, |d3| ≤ 5. The same direction counts as one.)
y-m-71-07.s.s2.hint.0: Write the perpendicularity conditions with m1 and m2 as equations in the components and check which component of d is fixed.
y-m-71-07.s.s2.hint.1: Write what relationship d must have with (0, 0, 1) to be perpendicular to α, and choose components that break that relationship.
y-m-71-07.s.s2.ok.c1: It is perpendicular to m1 and m2.
y-m-71-07.s.s2.fail.c1: It is not perpendicular to the direction vector (1, 0, 0) of m1.
y-m-71-07.s.s2.ok.c2: It is not parallel to the normal direction (0, 0, 1) of α.
y-m-71-07.s.s2.fail.c2: If d has the form (0, 0, d3), it is perpendicular to α, so it is not a counterexample.
y-m-71-07.s.s2.explain: d = (0, 1, 0), (0, 1, 1), (0, 1, 2) all have d1 = 0 so they are perpendicular to m1 and m2, but they are not parallel to (0, 0, 1), so they are not perpendicular to α. Since m1 and m2 are parallel, the same information was used twice.
y-m-71-07.s.s3.prompt: To conclude l ⟂ α, what information must be added to the information above?
y-m-71-07.s.s3.hint.0: Write, for each choice, whether it gives a new equation on the components of d.
y-m-71-07.s.s3.hint.1: Compare whether the new equation is the same information as d1 = 0 or different information.
y-m-71-07.s.s3.o.a: It is also perpendicular to another line in α that is parallel to the x-axis
y-m-71-07.s.s3.r.a: A line in the same direction as m1 and m2 gives no new equation. Compare whether it carries the same information as the previous two lines.
y-m-71-07.s.s3.o.b: l passes through a point outside α
y-m-71-07.s.s3.r.b: The position of a point does not change the equation of the direction vector. You need information about the direction, not about the point it passes through.
y-m-71-07.s.s3.o.c: It is also perpendicular to a line in α that is not parallel to the x-axis
y-m-71-07.s.s3.r.c: You understood that you need information about a line with a different direction in the plane. Two non-parallel lines in the same plane meet at one point.
y-m-71-07.s.s3.o.d: l meets m1 at one point
y-m-71-07.s.s3.r.d: Having an intersection point is information about position. It does not give a new equation about the direction.
y-m-71-07.s.s3.explain: If it is perpendicular to two non-parallel lines in the plane, it is perpendicular to the plane. For example, if it is also perpendicular to the y-axis direction (0, 1, 0), then d2 = 0 and d = (0, 0, d3).

y-m-71-08.title: Depending on the position of a point, how many tangents can be drawn?
y-m-71-08.topic: The number of tangents to a parabola
y-m-71-08.goal: Predict and revise the number of tangents that can be drawn from a point outside, on, and inside the parabola y² = 4x, and explain which tangent a solution that treats the slope as a letter misses.
y-m-71-08.material: Consider the parabola y² = 4x (read: y squared equals 4 x). Its vertex is O(0, 0), and the y-axis (x = 0) meets this parabola only at the vertex and is a tangent. We want to find out how many tangents can be drawn to this parabola from a point A on the coordinate plane. If the point is on the parabola, we count the tangent through that point. Lengths are written without units.
y-m-71-08.thinking.0: Predicting the number of tangents from the position of a point
y-m-71-08.thinking.1: Revising your judgment when a new point appears
y-m-71-08.thinking.2: Finding the cases a solution method misses
y-m-71-08.prereq.0: Assumption: this task is set at an advanced high-school level, to be solved after already learning the elective course 'Geometry' (conic sections, plane vectors, solids and space coordinates); 'H3' is only a difficulty label for this production batch and does not mean the course is assigned to a particular grade. The standard form of a parabola, the equation of a tangent (the tangent with slope m has the form y = mx + 1/m), the discriminant of a quadratic equation
y-m-71-08.s.s1.prompt: Points are revealed one at a time. Each time, predict the number of tangents that can be drawn from that point.
y-m-71-08.s.s1.hint.0: Put the coordinates of the point into y² = 4x and compare which of y² and 4x is larger.
y-m-71-08.s.s1.hint.1: Write the tangent with slope m as y = mx + 1/m, put in the coordinates of the point to make an equation in m, and check the sign of the discriminant.
y-m-71-08.s.s1.st.0.info: The point A(1, 3) is given. (Putting x = 1, y = 3 into y² = 4x gives 9 and 4, and 9 is larger.)
y-m-71-08.s.s1.st.0.ask: How many tangents can be drawn from A to the parabola?
y-m-71-08.s.s1.st.0.after: The tangent y = mx + 1/m through A(1, 3) satisfies 3 = m + 1/m, that is, m² − 3m + 1 = 0, whose discriminant is 5, positive, so there are two slopes. The point is outside, so there are 2 tangents.
y-m-71-08.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You thought there is only one tangent. Test whether you can find two different slopes of tangents through the point.
y-m-71-08.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You did not distinguish whether the point is outside or inside the parabola. Think about from which side tangents can be drawn.
y-m-71-08.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The memory that there are two tangents from an outside point and the comparison of the position of the point fit together.
y-m-71-08.s.s1.st.1.info: This time the point is B(1, 2). (y² = 4 and 4x = 4 are equal.)
y-m-71-08.s.s1.st.1.ask: How many tangents can be drawn from B?
y-m-71-08.s.s1.st.1.after: The tangent through B(1, 2) satisfies 2 = m + 1/m, that is, (m − 1)² = 0, so there is only one slope (m = 1). From a point on the parabola there is 1 tangent.
y-m-71-08.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You judged that from a point on the parabola there is only the tangent at that point.
y-m-71-08.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You carried over the conclusion for the outside point. This point is on the parabola, so the position has changed.
y-m-71-08.s.s1.st.1.r.c: From a point on the parabola there is a line tangent at that point. Check whether there is a tangent through the point.
y-m-71-08.s.s1.st.2.info: The point is C(4, 1). (4x = 16 is greater than y² = 1.)
y-m-71-08.s.s1.st.2.ask: How many tangents can be drawn from C?
y-m-71-08.s.s1.st.2.after: The tangent through C(4, 1) satisfies 1 = 4m + 1/m, that is, 4m² − m + 1 = 0, and the discriminant is 1 − 16 < 0, so there is no slope. From a point inside, no tangent can be drawn.
y-m-71-08.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You carried over the conclusion for a point on the parabola. This point is not on the parabola.
y-m-71-08.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You judged that it is a point inside the parabola, so there are no tangents at all.
y-m-71-08.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You carried over the conclusion for the outside point. Compare the sizes of 4x and y² to check whether it is inside.
y-m-71-08.s.s1.reflect: The numbers of tangents at the three points were 2, 1 and 0. How can you state the position of a point in terms of comparing the sizes of y² and 4x? Also think about how this comparison connects to the sign of the discriminant.
y-m-71-08.s.s2.prompt: How many tangents can be drawn to the parabola from the point D(0, 3)? Also write which tangent, if any, a solution that sets the slope as m can miss.
y-m-71-08.s.s2.hint.0: Write how the equation a·m² − b·m + 1 = 0 in m changes when the x-coordinate of D is 0.
y-m-71-08.s.s2.hint.1: Find which line through a point with x-coordinate 0 cannot be written in the form y = mx + n.
y-m-71-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did I explain in my own words how the equation changes in the solution that sets the slope as m?
y-m-71-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did I distinguish a tangent that has a slope from a tangent whose slope cannot be used?
y-m-71-08.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did I check that the tangents I wrote really pass through D(0, 3)?
y-m-71-08.s.s2.model.0: 2. Putting (0, 3) into y = mx + 1/m gives 3 = 1/m, so only the one tangent y = x/3 + 3 with slope 1/3 comes out, but the y-axis (x = 0), which has no slope, is also a tangent at the vertex, so together there are 2.
y-m-71-08.s.s2.model.1: There are two tangents. This is possible because point D is outside the parabola, and one is x = 0 and the other is y = (1/3)x + 3. x = 0 cannot be written in the form y = mx + n, so it is missed by the solution that uses the slope.

y-m-71-09.title: When projected, is the area cosθ times or cos²θ times?
y-m-71-09.goal: Test one of two models with numbers for a concrete figure, and explain why the reason 'all sides shrink' is wrong by separating the sides parallel to the line where the two planes meet from the sides perpendicular to it.
y-m-71-09.material: In space coordinates, triangle ABC has vertices A(0, 0, 0), B(4, 0, 0), C(0, 4, 4). The angle θ between the plane of this triangle and the xy-plane is 45°, and cos45° ≈ 0.707. The shadow (orthogonal projection) of this triangle dropped perpendicularly onto the xy-plane is the triangle with vertices A(0, 0), B(4, 0), C'(0, 4). Jihu said, 'Lengths shrink to cosθ times, so both the width and the height shrink, and the area becomes cos²θ times,' and Seoa said, 'The area becomes cosθ times.' Lengths are written without units.
y-m-71-09.thinking.1: Finding the weak link in the supporting claim
y-m-71-09.thinking.2: Explaining by connecting the changes of the sides and of the area
y-m-71-09.prereq.0: Assumption: this task is set at an advanced high-school level, to be solved after already learning the elective course 'Geometry' (conic sections, plane vectors, solids and space coordinates); 'H3' is only a difficulty label for this production batch and does not mean the course is assigned to a particular grade. Space coordinates, the angle between two planes, the meaning of orthogonal projection and the basic ideas of projected length and area
y-m-71-09.s.s1.prompt: The area of triangle ABC is 8√2 ≈ 11.31 and the area of the projection is 8. What can this one example tell us about the two claims?
y-m-71-09.s.s1.hint.0: Put θ = 45° into the formulas of the two claims and predict the area of the projection for each.
y-m-71-09.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the two predicted values side by side with the actual area of the projection, 8.
y-m-71-09.s.s1.o.a: Jihu's cos²θ times is right. Because 0.707 is cos²45°
y-m-71-09.s.s1.r.a: cos²45° is 0.5. You did not check by calculation which formula 0.707 is the value of.
y-m-71-09.s.s1.o.b: It agrees with Seoa's cosθ times. One example alone is not a proof, so I will check with other figures too
y-m-71-09.s.s1.r.b: You confirmed that it agrees with Seoa's model and also thought about the limit of a single example.
y-m-71-09.s.s1.o.c: Both claims are wrong. Because 0.707 is different from cos45°
y-m-71-09.s.s1.r.c: You did not check from the data that cos45° is about 0.707.
y-m-71-09.s.s1.o.d: It agrees with Seoa's cosθ times and disagrees with Jihu's cos²θ times
y-m-71-09.s.s1.r.d: This is a judgment made by calculating the values the two models predict and comparing them with the actual value.
y-m-71-09.s.s1.explain: The actual ratio 8 ÷ 8√2 ≈ 0.707 equals cos45° ≈ 0.707 and differs from cos²45° = 0.5. This one example agrees with Seoa's model, but one example cannot show that it holds for every figure.
y-m-71-09.s.s1.acc.0: It agrees with Seoa's model, and the caution of wanting to check with other figures because it is just one example has been added. This is accepted here.
y-m-71-09.s.s2.prompt: Here is a new figure. The rectangle PQRS has vertices P(0, 0, 0), Q(2, 0, 0), R(2, 3, 3), S(0, 3, 3). Side PQ has length 2 and is still 2 after projecting. Side QR has length 3√2 and is 3 after projecting. How can you evaluate Jihu's reason 'all lengths shrink to cosθ times' for this figure?
y-m-71-09.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate separately the ratio of the projected length to the original length for PQ and for QR.
y-m-71-09.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether multiplying the two ratios equals the ratio of the areas.
y-m-71-09.s.s2.o.a: It does not hold. There is a side whose length stays the same
y-m-71-09.s.s2.r.a: You found from the data that how much a side shrinks differs depending on its direction.
y-m-71-09.s.s2.o.b: It holds. Both PQ and QR shrink when projected
y-m-71-09.s.s2.r.b: You did not check how the length of PQ changes. It stays 2 to 2.
y-m-71-09.s.s2.o.c: It does not hold. When projected, all sides actually get longer
y-m-71-09.s.s2.r.c: No side gets longer. Compare the original length and the projected length for each side.
y-m-71-09.s.s2.o.d: It cannot be judged. It is a rectangle, so it differs from the triangle before
y-m-71-09.s.s2.r.d: Even if the name of the figure differs, you can compare side lengths. This is a case that the data is enough to judge.
y-m-71-09.s.s2.explain: PQ is parallel to the line where the two planes meet (the x-axis), so its length stays the same, and only QR shrinks to cosθ times (3√2 → 3). So the reason 'all sides become cosθ times' is wrong. The area goes 6√2 → 6, about 0.707 times, the same as the effect of shrinking in only one direction.
y-m-71-09.s.s3.prompt: How would you explain it to Jihu? Using the two figures above, write with numbers how the side lengths changed and why the area is cosθ times and not cos²θ times.
y-m-71-09.s.s3.hint.0: Write in a table the lengths of PQ and QR before and after projection.
y-m-71-09.s.s3.hint.1: Looking at the table, write in one sentence which direction shrinks and which stays the same.
y-m-71-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I write in my own words that one direction stays the same and only the other direction shrinks?
y-m-71-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Do the numbers I wrote (for example 8√2 → 8, 6√2 → 6, 2 → 2, 3√2 → 3) agree with the data above?
y-m-71-09.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I compare what the ratio of the areas would have been if both directions had shrunk?
y-m-71-09.s.s3.model.0: A direction parallel to the line where the two planes meet, like PQ, keeps its length when projected, and only the direction perpendicular to it becomes cosθ times. So the area is cosθ times, not cos²θ times. In this example too, 6√2 becomes 6, about 0.7 times.
y-m-71-09.s.s3.model.1: Side PQ did not change from 2 to 2. Only side QR shrank from 3√2 to 3, so the ratio is 1/√2. If both sides had shrunk, the ratio would have to be 1/2, but the actual area ratio is 6/(6√2), about 0.7, so it does not fit.
